passage: I'm Sabina, Tarun's classmate. The plants test was over and nobody had to learn anything more, but Tarun kept going. At recess I saw him on his knees by the school wall, watching a line of ants carrying rice. He had a notebook that wasn't for any subject. He'd drawn the line and written, "Do they follow a smell? Test: rub finger across path." He did it, and the ants got muddled, walking in circles. Then he asked Sir how ants smell without noses. Sir said, "Look it up." He went to the library that same day. I'm not sure why he cares so much, but he looked happy.

qa.q: What did Tarun write in his notebook as a test?
qa.a: "Rub finger across path."

qa.q: What does Tarun going to the library that same day suggest?
qa.a: He was genuinely curious and wanted to find the answer himself, even though it was not for any test.

qa.q: How could Sir support Tarun's curiosity more?
qa.a: Besides saying "look it up," he could invite Tarun to share what he found with the class or suggest another small experiment.

qa.q: How does Sabina see Tarun's interest?
qa.a: Sabina notices it but doesn't fully understand why he cares so much, though she can tell it makes him happy.

grounding: It shows, through a classmate's eyes, a boy investigating ants with his own questions beyond what school required.

passage:
Monday: The science chapter only said, "The moon has phases." Swati, eleven, frowned. "But why?" Her sister Pooja shrugged. "It's not in the exam."
Thursday: Swati borrowed a torch and an orange. In the dark bedroom she held the orange at arm's length and turned slowly while Pooja shone the torch. "Look, only half is lit, and I see different bits as I turn!"
The next week: Swati kept a moon diary, drawing the shape every night from the terrace. At the bottom she added her own question: "Why do we always see the same face?" Pooja started coming up to the terrace too.

qa.q: What did Swati use to model the moon?
qa.a: A torch and an orange.

qa.q: Why did Swati frown at the chapter's one line?
qa.a: She wanted to understand the reason behind the phases, and the bare statement did not satisfy her curiosity.

qa.q: What would you advise a teacher who hears Swati's new question?
qa.a: Welcome it, perhaps point her to a book or ask her to model it with the orange again, instead of saying it is outside the syllabus.

qa.q: How did Pooja's view change over the week?
qa.a: She began by saying it wasn't in the exam but ended up joining Swati on the terrace, drawn in by her sister's curiosity. 🙂

grounding: It shows a girl's own questions about the moon driving her to investigate far beyond the textbook line.

passage: Chetan, you ask why I still open every machine. When I was ten, the clock in our kitchen in Nashik stopped. Our teacher had told us nothing about clocks; it was in no book. But I wanted to know what made it tick. One Sunday I took it apart on a newspaper, laying every screw in a line so I would remember the order. Inside were little wheels with teeth, biting into each other. I asked the watch repairman in the market a hundred questions. He laughed and showed me the spring. When I put it back, it ticked. My mother didn't scold. She only asked, "Sarita, my girl, what will you open next?"

qa.q: Where did young Sarita take the clock apart?
qa.a: On a newspaper, one Sunday.

qa.q: Why did Sarita want to open the clock at ten?
qa.a: She wanted to know what made it tick, out of her own curiosity, since nothing at school asked her to.

qa.q: Which of her choices helped her investigate carefully?
qa.a: Laying the screws in a line helped her remember the order, and asking the repairman gave her expert help.

qa.q: How might Sarita's mother have seen the opened clock?
qa.a: Instead of worrying about a broken clock, she seemed to see a curious child and encouraged more exploring.

grounding: It shows, told by an elder, a ten-year-old's self-driven investigation of how a clock works.

passage: The Hindi test was tomorrow, and Aditi had promised Amma she would revise. But a line of ants was marching across the kitchen wall, and she could not stop watching. Why did they all follow the same path? She put a grain of sugar a little off the line. One ant found it, then more came. 'Imran, look! They're telling each other!' Her brother groaned. 'Test, Aditi.' She revised for an hour, then wrote in the back of her notebook: 'Do ants leave a smell trail? Ask library.' On Saturday she borrowed a book on insects that nobody had assigned.

qa.q: Where did Aditi place the grain of sugar?
qa.a: She put it a little off the ants' line on the kitchen wall.

qa.q: What does Aditi writing a question in her notebook suggest about her?
qa.a: It suggests her curiosity was strong and her own, so she wanted to keep investigating even after the test pressure.

qa.q: How could Aditi balance her curiosity with schoolwork?
qa.a: She could do as she did here: note her question down, finish revising, and explore it later when she has time.

qa.q: How might Imran see his sister's ant experiment?
qa.a: He seems mildly annoyed that she is distracted, but he may also be a little curious about what she found.

grounding: Illustrates a child's own drive to question and investigate beyond school requirements, despite a test the next day.

passage: From her balcony in their Bengaluru apartment, Mehak had watched pigeons for a week. Why did their heads bob when they walked? None of her textbooks said. She tried walking with her head bobbing and felt silly. She asked her uncle, Vijay, who shrugged. 'Ask the internet.' Instead, Mehak filmed a pigeon on his phone, slowed it down and noticed the head stayed still for a moment, then jerked forward. 'It's like they're taking photos!' she said. She made a small chart of her findings and pinned it above her desk, though no teacher would ever see it.

qa.q: Whose phone did Mehak use to film the pigeon?
qa.a: She used her uncle Vijay's phone.

qa.q: Why did Mehak keep investigating even though no teacher would see her chart?
qa.a: She was driven by her own curiosity and enjoyed finding the answer for its own sake.

qa.q: What could Vijay do to encourage Mehak's inquiry next time?
qa.a: He could ask her what she thinks is happening and help her test it, rather than just shrugging.

qa.q: How might a science teacher react if Mehak showed her chart?
qa.a: The teacher would likely be delighted and might invite Mehak to share it with the class. 🙂

grounding: Shows a child's intrinsic curiosity leading her to investigate a question no school task required.

passage:
"Chacha, why does the moon follow our car?" Harish asked from the back seat.
Yogesh laughed. "Does it?"
"It does! The trees go backwards, but the moon stays with us."
"What do you think?"
Harish, ten, pressed his face to the window. "Maybe because it's very far? Like when I walk, the far hills don't move either."
"Good guess. Want to check?"
"We didn't do this in school."
"So?"
The next evening Harish dragged his uncle to the colony library, found a book on the night sky, and read the page out loud twice. "It's the distance! I was right!"
Then he asked, "But why is it sometimes orange?"

qa.q: Where did Harish take his uncle the next evening?
qa.a: To the colony library.

qa.q: What was Harish feeling when he shouted "I was right!"?
qa.a: He felt excited and proud that his own guess about distance was confirmed.

qa.q: What did Yogesh do that fed Harish's curiosity?
qa.a: He asked what Harish thought and offered to check, instead of just giving the answer.

qa.q: How might Yogesh feel when Harish asks the next question about the orange moon?
qa.a: Amused and pleased, seeing that one answer only made Harish more curious.

grounding: Shows a child asking a deep question beyond his syllabus and investigating it on his own.

passage: I'm Afreen, and last summer I watched a line of ants carry a dead beetle across our balcony for an hour. Nobody told me to. I wanted to know how they decided where to go. I started a notebook called "Questions Nobody Asked Me". I wrote: Do ants talk? Why do they walk in lines? Payal Didi, the librarian, found me a book on insects, and I learned about scent trails. Now the notebook has forty-two questions. My teacher says they're not in the syllabus. I don't care. Some days I find one answer and three new questions.

qa.q: What did Afreen call the notebook?
qa.a: "Questions Nobody Asked Me".

qa.q: Why did Afreen keep watching the ants for an hour?
qa.a: Afreen was curious and fascinated, wanting to understand how the ants decided where to go.

qa.q: What would you advise Afreen to try next with the notebook?
qa.a: Pick one question and set up a simple safe experiment, like watching where ants go after a sugar trail.

qa.q: How might Payal Didi see Afreen's questions?
qa.a: Payal Didi would likely feel delighted to help a child who reads for the joy of finding out.

grounding: Shows a child's own drive to ask questions and investigate beyond school requirements.

passage:
Science teacher's note, Pradeep, October
Zainab (9) stayed after class twice this week. The first time she asked why leaves change colour, which isn't in our syllabus until next year. I told her a little about chlorophyll and asked what she noticed on her way home. On Friday she came back with a bag of leaves sorted from green to brown, and a new question: "Why does the neem stay green?" I've lent her a book and suggested she ask her grandfather, who grows plants. I'll give her five minutes at Monday's assembly to show the leaves.

qa.q: What did Zainab bring back on Friday?
qa.a: A bag of leaves sorted from green to brown.

qa.q: What does Zainab staying after class suggest about her?
qa.a: She feels a strong, curious pull to understand things, even when no marks depend on it.

qa.q: Why is Pradeep's plan for Monday's assembly a good step?
qa.a: It shows Zainab her curiosity is valued and may spark questions in other children too.

qa.q: How might Zainab's grandfather feel when she asks him about the neem?
qa.a: He would probably be pleased and proud to share what he knows with a curious grandchild.

grounding: Shows a child's inquiry beyond the syllabus, noticed and encouraged by her science teacher.

passage:
Thursday. Jatin's diary.
The moon was orange tonight, low over the water tank. Nobody at school asked us about it, but I couldn't stop wondering why. Is it hot? Is it closer? I asked Sahil from the next building and he said, "Maybe it's dust?" That wasn't enough. After dinner I found Papa's old sky book and read three pages. It says the light passes through more air near the ground, so the blue gets scattered and the orange is left. I drew it with arrows. Now I want to know why sunsets do the same thing. Tomorrow I'm checking at sunset with Sahil.

qa.q: Where was the moon when Jatin saw it?
qa.a: Low over the water tank.

qa.q: How did Jatin feel when Sahil's answer "Maybe it's dust?" wasn't enough?
qa.a: Jatin felt curious and unsatisfied, so kept searching for a proper explanation.

qa.q: What could help Jatin keep exploring questions like this?
qa.a: Jatin could keep a question notebook and test ideas, such as watching the sunset with Sahil as planned.

qa.q: How might Sahil feel about checking the sunset with Jatin?
qa.a: Sahil might feel intrigued and pleased to be part of Jatin's investigation.

grounding: A child investigates an orange moon with a book and plans a sunset check, though no one at school asked.

passage: Before the rains came to Pipariya, Uma noticed long lines of ants carrying grain up the wall of the cowshed. "Why are they all going up?" she asked her cousin Akash. He shrugged. "Ants are ants." Uma wasn't satisfied. For three evenings she sat by the wall after school with a notebook, not for any homework. She left a pinch of sugar low and a pinch high. The ants took the high one first. When the first storm hit, the low floor flooded, and the ants' line stayed dry. "They knew!" Uma shouted. Akash came over, frowning at the dry line, and asked, "Show me."

qa.q: Where were the ants carrying grain?
qa.a: Up the wall of the cowshed.

qa.q: What does Uma shouting "They knew!" suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt excited and thrilled that her own experiment seemed to explain the ants' behaviour.

qa.q: What could an adult do to encourage Uma's curiosity?
qa.a: They could give her a magnifying glass or a simple book about insects, and ask her what she wants to test next.

qa.q: How does Akash's view of the ants change?
qa.a: At first he thinks they aren't worth thinking about, but by the end he is intrigued and wants to see.

grounding: A village girl investigates ants moving grain before the rains through her own experiment, beyond schoolwork.

passage: Every hour, the old clock in Prague's square rang and little wooden figures marched out. Jana, eleven, had seen it a hundred times. This spring she started asking questions no teacher had set: how did the figures know when to move? What turned the wheels? She and her friend Wanjiru spent their Saturday in the city museum reading about gears and weights. Jana copied a drawing of the mechanism, filling two notebook pages. Wanjiru yawned. "It's just a clock." "But how does it know?" Jana said, already sketching another question in the margin.

qa.q: How did Jana and Wanjiru spend their Saturday?
qa.a: In the city museum reading about gears and weights.

qa.q: What was Jana feeling as she filled two notebook pages about the mechanism?
qa.a: She felt absorbed and curious, eager to understand the clock for her own sake, since no teacher had set these questions.

qa.q: How could Jana's family support her interest?
qa.a: They could help her find books or a workshop visit about how clocks and gears work.

qa.q: How does Wanjiru see Jana's interest in the clock?
qa.a: Wanjiru seems bored and thinks it's just a clock, while Jana finds it exciting.

grounding: An eleven-year-old spends a Saturday researching the gears of an old clock out of her own curiosity.

passage:
At the Thursday science club, Aadhya, ten, raised her hand before Naveen Sir had even finished the attendance.

"Sir, why does the moon look huge when it's rising and small when it's high up?"

Naveen Sir smiled. "It's not in our syllabus. What do you think?"

"Maybe it's closer when it rises?"

"How could you check?"

That week, Aadhya held a one-rupee coin at arm's length every evening and covered the moon with it, once low over the buildings and once high in the sky. The coin covered it both times.

"It's the same size!" she told the club the next Thursday. "So why does it look bigger?"

Naveen Sir handed her a library book on illusions. She read it on the bus home.

qa.q: What did Aadhya use to cover the moon?
qa.a: She held a one-rupee coin at arm's length.

qa.q: How did Aadhya feel when the coin covered the moon both times?
qa.a: Aadhya felt surprised and excited, and even more curious about why it looked bigger.

qa.q: How did Naveen Sir support Aadhya's curiosity?
qa.a: He asked what she thought and how she could check, then gave her a book, so she investigated herself.

qa.q: How might the other club members react to Aadhya's findings?
qa.a: They might be surprised and curious too, wanting to try the coin test themselves.

grounding: At a school science club, a child asks a question beyond the syllabus and investigates it on her own.

passage:
I'm Lokesh, Afreen's big brother. During the monsoon, our garden in Pune fills with snails, and this year my sister, nine, got obsessed.

Every morning she went out with an old notebook and a torch. She wrote down how many snails were on the wall, the steps and the tulsi pot. She asked me why they came out after rain and hid in the sun. I didn't know.

She borrowed my phone to look it up, then found a library book about molluscs. Nobody asked her to. It wasn't homework.

By August, her notebook had drawings of shells, dates, and arrows. I'm not sure what she felt, but she was up before anyone else every day.

qa.q: Where did Afreen count the snails?
qa.a: She counted the snails on the wall, the steps and the tulsi pot.

qa.q: What might Afreen have been feeling during the monsoon mornings?
qa.a: Lokesh couldn't be sure, but she seemed curious and eager, getting up before anyone else.

qa.q: How could the family encourage Afreen's inquiry?
qa.a: Give her time and books, ask about her notebook, and help her find answers to her questions.

qa.q: How does Lokesh see his sister's snail project?
qa.a: Lokesh is impressed and a little puzzled, noticing she did it without being asked.

grounding: An older brother observes his sister investigating snails in the monsoon out of curiosity, beyond homework.

passage:
First week of winter: Dhruv, eleven, notices frost on the car roof in the Shimla colony, but not on the car under the tree. He asks his sister Trisha why. She shrugs.

Two weeks later: Dhruv checks every morning and writes down which cars have frost. He finds that cars under trees or roofs rarely do. He asks his science teacher, who says, "Keep looking."

Christmas week: Dhruv reads about heat escaping to the open sky at night. He explains it to Trisha at breakfast, drawing arrows on a napkin. "The tree is like a blanket!"

Trisha laughs. "You did all that for frost?"

"Yes. And next I want to know why snow squeaks."

qa.q: Which cars rarely had frost?
qa.a: Cars under trees or roofs rarely did.

qa.q: How did Dhruv feel explaining the frost to Trisha?
qa.a: Dhruv felt excited and proud to have found the answer, and eager for the next question.

qa.q: How could the teacher keep supporting Dhruv's curiosity?
qa.a: The teacher could encourage his observations and suggest ways to test his next question.

qa.q: How does Trisha see Dhruv's investigation?
qa.a: Trisha finds it amusing and surprising that he did so much work for frost.

grounding: Over winter weeks, a child investigates why frost forms only on some cars, beyond any school requirement.

passage: Zeenat, you asked why old Sudha Aunty still keeps a notebook of questions. Let me tell you. The winter I was ten, fog sat on our village for weeks, and I noticed the dew on the spider webs vanished by noon but stayed in the shade of the well. Nobody at school taught that. So every morning I checked three webs, one sunny, one shady, one near the stove smoke, and wrote down when the drops went. My brother Kishan called me mad. Then the science master saw my notebook and lent me his own book on weather. I read it under the quilt by lantern light. That notebook was the first of forty.

qa.q: How many webs did Sudha check every morning?
qa.a: She checked three webs, one sunny, one shady, one near the stove smoke.

qa.q: Why did young Sudha keep checking the webs every morning?
qa.a: She was curious and fascinated by why the dew lasted longer in the shade, and wanted to find out for herself.

qa.q: What turning point came when the science master saw Sudha's notebook?
qa.a: By lending her his own book on weather, he encouraged her to keep investigating, and that notebook became the first of forty.

qa.q: How did Kishan see his sister's web-checking?
qa.a: Kishan thought it was mad, probably not understanding why anyone would study dew without being told to.

grounding: Shows a child's own drive to investigate a question about dew beyond anything taught at school, told as an elder's memory.
